title: SPA/307/2016 of Vinay Kumar AND ANOTHER Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Special Appeal No. 307 of 2016
Vinay Kumar & another. ............ Appellants

Advocates for the appellants:

Advocates for the party respondents:
Mr. A.S. Rawat, Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr. Kanti Ram Sharma, Advocate;
Mr. B.P. Nautiyal, Senior Advocate; Mr. Arvind Vashistha, Senior Advocate, assisted
by Mr. Shailendra Nauriyal, Advocate; Mr. D.K. Joshi; Mr. Rajesh Joshi; Mr. V.P.
Bahuguna; Mr. Rakesh Kumar Joshi; Mr. Shiv Pande; Mr. Rajesh Pandey; Mr. Deep
Prakash Bhatt; Mr. D.C.S. Rawat; Mr. Rajendra Singh Azad; Mr. Tapan Singh; Mr.
V.K. Kaparwan.
Mr. M.C. Pande, Addl. Advocate General, with Mr. Narayan Dutt, Brief Holder for
the State of Uttarakhand.

JUDGMENT
Coram: Hon'ble K.M. Joseph, C.J.
 Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
 Dated: 29th May, 2018

3
K.M. JOSEPH, C.J. (Oral)
 Since these appeals are connected and involve identical questions
of fact and law, we are disposing of the same by this common judgment.
2. All these appeals are directed against the judgment passed by the
learned Single Judge in Writ Petition (S/S) No. 844 of 2016. Special
Appeal No. 307 of 2016 has been filed by writ petitioner Nos. 1 & 2 in the
said writ petition. Special Appeal No. 301 of 2016 has been filed by
petitioner No. 3 in the said writ petition. All the other appeals have been
filed, on the basis of the leave granted, by persons, who are apparently
similarly circumstanced as the writ petitioners and they would appear to
adopt the line of arguments of the writ petitioners.
3. The reliefs, which were sought in the writ petition, are as follows:
"(i) To issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
directing the respondent authorities, more pertinently the
respondent no. 3 to carry out scrutiny of the forms and
candidature of the those candidates for cancelling the
candidature, who passed their C-TET Examinations after 1st
January 2012 through C-TET 2012, 2013, 2014 & 2015
examinations conducted by CBSE and obtained certificates
fraudulently and then eliminate their names from the final
select list and thereafter issue a fresh modified final select list
in accordance with rules and the notification dated 17-02-
2016.
(ii) To issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
directing the respondent authorities, more pertinently
respondent no. 3 to carry out scrutiny of the forms and
candidature of the candidates, who were already appointed
on the post of Primary teacher in the government primary
schools and were ineligible for being selection in terms of
GO dated 16-02-2016 and condition dated 7 (N) of the
advertisement dated 17-02-2016.
(iii) To issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
directing the respondent no. 3 to prepare a fresh result of
selection by sieving out the ineligible candidates who have
been declared successful and selected on account of
suppression, concealment and by playing fraud in as much as
though already appointed on the post of primary teacher in a
government school, have again participated in the selection
process irrespective of GO dated 16-02-2016 and condition
no. 7(N) of advertisement dated 17-02-2016.

4
(iv) To issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of the
certiorari quashing the selection of all such candidates who
have participated in the selection process initiated vide
notification dated 17-02-2016 by concealing and suppressing
the fact that they were already appointed on the post of
primary teacher in a government primary school or procured
wrong C-TET Certificates pertaining to C-TET 2012, 2013,
2014 & 2015.
(v) To issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
directing the respondent no. 3 to prepare a fresh result of
selection by sieving out the ineligible candidates who have
been declared successful and selected on account of
suppression, concealment and by playing fraud."
4. Briefly put, the case of the writ petitioners was as follows:
 Notification dated 17.02.2016 was issued and it was also, later,
amended by Notification dated 05.03.2016. Both the Notifications are
together produced as Annexure No. 1. The purport of the Notification
was setting in motion the recruitment process for appointment to the posts
of Assistant Teacher (Primary) in the Government Primary Schools in the
State of Uttarakhand. The writ petitioners have passed B.Ed. They are
Graduates also. Reference is made to the Right of Children to Free and
Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (hereinafter referred to as the "2009
Act"). Reliance is placed on Notification dated 23.08.2010 issued by
NCTE. In regard to Classes 1 to 5, the minimum qualifications were
stipulated by NCTE. It is the case of the writ petitioners that NCTE, vide
Notification dated 23.08.2010, also permitted B.Ed. degree holders to be
appointed as Assistant Teacher (Primary) up to 01.01.2012. After 2011,
B.Ed. degree holders could not be appointed as Assistant Teacher
(Primary) for Classes 1 to 5 for the whole of the country. The actual
qualification for Classes 1 to 5, otherwise, was Diploma in Elementary
Education with various academic qualifications and pass in the Teachers'
Eligibility Test (hereinafter referred to as "TET") to be conducted by the
appropriate Government in accordance with the guidelines as framed by
NCTE for the purpose. It is stated that TET was started for the first time
in the year 2011. Therefore, when NCTE issued Notification dated
23.08.2010, under Clause (3), it had also permitted B.Ed. degree holders

5
to participate in TET examination pertaining to Classes 1 to 5 in Central
as well as State TET. Thereafter, it is the case of the writ petitioners that
only those candidates, who were having minimum qualification as per
Clause (1) of the Notification, were permitted to appear for CTET. In
short, no B.Ed. degree holder was entitled to appear for CTET after
01.01.2012 as per Notification dated 23.08.2010. It is their further case,
however, that, though B.Ed. degree holders in the State of Uttarakhand
were permitted to be appointed by virtue of various Notifications issued
lastly till 31.03.2016, only those B.Ed. degree holders, who had obtained
TET from the State of Uttarakhand, and also only those CTET holders,
who had obtained CTET up to 2012, were eligible to be considered for
selection. It is their case that, however, when the select list was prepared,
the persons, who had obtained CTET even after 2012, have also been
included in the select list. It is on this basis that the reliefs were sought.
5. This writ petition came to be considered along with the batch of
other writ petitions before the learned Single Judge with which this Court
may not be concerned and the actual judgment, insofar as it relates to Writ
Petition (S/S) No. 844 of 2016, is seen contained in paragraph 28 of the
common judgment rendered. Since the judgment is contained in the said
paragraph 28, which is debated, we deem it appropriate to refer to the
same and extract it as follows:
"28. So far as WPSS No. 844 of 2016 is concerned, the
petitioner has prayed that many of the candidates who have been
selected or allowed to participate have actually not done their TET,
but some of them have done CTET i.e. Central Teachers Eligibility
Test after 2011 which was not permissible under law. This
contention of the petitioner, on the face of it, does not appear to be
correct as it is the Central Government Body i.e. NCTE which has
allowed B.Ed. qualified candidates to take part in the selection
process till 31.3.2016. By necessary implication, therefore, if such
candidates have passed their TET after 2011 apparently there seems
to be no anomaly unless there was any specific restriction on this
and it is the selection committee who will look into this aspect
before issuing appointment letters to such candidates.
Consequently, Writ Petition No. 844 of 2016 has no merit and the
same is hereby dismissed."

6
6. It is necessary to notice certain developments, which took place
upon the filing of the appeals. It was submitted that a number of persons,
who are CTET, have actually been appointed in the meantime. The list
was provided by the State Government. Thereupon, appellants were
directed to take steps to implead the persons, who were appointed, and,
thus, it is that a large number of party respondents have been impleaded in
all the appeals.
7. We heard Mr. Subhash Upadhyaya, learned counsel, who appears
on behalf of the appellants in Special Appeal Nos. 307 of 2016, 52 of
2017 and 13 of 2017. We also heard Mr. Vinay Kumar, learned counsel,
who appears on behalf of the appellants in Special Appeal Nos. 247 of
2016 and 65 of 2017, who were not the writ petitioners in the writ
petition, but who have filed the appeals on the basis of leave. Equally, we
heard Mr. Bhagwat Mehra, learned counsel, who, as noted, appears on
behalf of the appellant in Special Appeal No. 301 of 2016 filed by the
third petitioner in the writ petition, and also on behalf of the appellants in
other connected appeal, namely, Special Appeal No. 302 of 2016 filed
after obtaining leave. We also heard Mr. K.P. Upadhyaya, learned
counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants in Special Appeal No. 100
of 2017.
8. On behalf of the party respondents, we heard Mr. A.S. Rawat,
Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr. Kanti Ram Sharma, Advocate; Mr. B.P.
Nautiyal, Senior Advocate; Mr. Arvind Vashistha, Senior Advocate,
assisted by Mr. Shailendra Nauriyal, Advocate; Mr. D.K. Joshi; Mr.
Rajesh Joshi; Mr. Rakesh Kumar Joshi; Mr. Shiv Pande; Mr. Rajesh
Pandey; Mr. Deep Prakash Bhatt; Mr. D.C.S. Rawat; Mr. Rajendra Singh
Azad; Mr. Tapan Singh; and Mr. V.K. Kaparwan. We also heard Mr.
M.C. Pande, learned Additional Advocate General appearing for the State
and Mr. Yogesh Pacholia, learned counsel appearing for NCTE.
9. Mr. Subhash Upadhyaya, learned counsel for the appellants, would
contend and stress his arguments, with reference to paragraph 28 of the

7
impugned judgment, which we have extracted, that the learned Single
Judge has erred in taking the view that, by implication, the persons, who
are B.Ed. degree holders and, for whom, NCTE has given exemption in
the State of Uttarakhand to vie for selection to the posts of Assistant
Teacher (Primary), are also to be treated as given benefit of eligibility to
participate in CTET. He would take us through the documents for the
years from 2012 onwards issued by CBSE. He was at pains to point out
that a perusal of the same would show that conspicuous by its absence in
the said documents is eligibility for B.Ed. degree holders to participate in
CTET. He would submit that, as far as the persons, who obtained TET
conducted by the State of Uttarakhand, are concerned, it is a different
matter altogether, as their case is based on different footsteps. In fact,
appellants have also obtained TET from the State of Uttarakhand. This,
according to him, is not impermissible; but, what was clearly
impermissible was permitting B.Ed. degree holders to take CTET after the
year 2011 made eligible for selection for Assistant Teacher (Primary).
Therefore, the sum and substance of his arguments can be summed-up as
follows:
 He proceeds to argue that though on the basis that, on the strength
of the Notifications issued by NCTE, B.Ed. degree holders were eligible
to be considered for appointment to the posts of Assistant Teacher
(Primary). He also does not have a dispute that such B.Ed. degree holders
could pass TET conducted by the State Government. The only point,
which arises, is whether those CTET holders, who have passed CTET
conducted by CBSE after the year 2011, could stake a claim for being
considered for appointment having regard to the various Notifications,
which have been issued by CBSE. His submission is that, clearly, they
were not eligible. If they had been selected on the strength of such a
certificate issued after 2011, it is illegal.
10. Mr. Vinay Kumar, learned counsel for the appellants in other cases,
would also adopt the same line of arguments as of Mr. Subhash
Upadhyaya. He would also join issue and point out that the applications

8
for participating in CTET are filed online. CBSE would not be in a
position to check the credentials of the candidates. It is rather for the
candidates who would have to check whether they were eligible to
participate in CTET. A candidate from Uttarakhand participating in
CTET, though he was not eligible, would be guilty of fraud and the matter
goes to the root of the appointment. The State Government was duty
bound to verify these aspects. Though there was, in fact, a direction that
the matter should be looked into, apparently, it has not been considered.
He would also take exception to the findings contained in paragraph 28 of
the judgment, which we have referred to.
11. Mr. K.P. Upadhyaya, learned counsel for the appellants in
connected case, also adopts the similar line of arguments. Equally does
Mr. Bhagwat Mehra.
12. Mr. A.S. Rawat, learned Senior Counsel appearing for some of the
private respondents, would, on the other hand, point out that the
appellants had participated in the test. The result was published on
27.03.2016 prior to filing of the writ petition. The writ petition was filed
on 25.04.2016. None of the respondents, who stood selected as Assistant
Teacher (Primary), were arrayed in the writ petition as party respondents.
He would invoke the principle that there cannot be approbation and
reprobation. He drew our attention to Section 23(2) of the 2009 Act. He
would point out that, under Notification dated 23.08.2010, B.Ed. degree
holders were rendered eligible by NCTE itself till 01.01.2012. In
Uttarakhand, a problem arose on account of non-availability of teachers
having the minimum qualification. The State Government wrote to
NCTE and power under Section 23(2) of the 2009 Act was invoked.
NCTE exercised power under Section 23(2) and permitted B.Ed. degree
holders to participate in the selection. This extension lasted till
31.03.2016. He would point out that guidelines have been framed by
NCTE and, in terms of the same, the party respondents were entitled to be
considered on the basis of CTET, which they had passed. He also points
out the rules, which have been framed and which have also been produced

9
along with the writ petition. He would point out clause 7.3 of the same, as
per which, according to him, B.Ed. degree holders were also rendered
eligible. The said clause 7.3 reads as follows:
 "7.3 Note:
(i) Relaxation up to 5% in the qualifying marks in the
minimum Educational Qualification for eligibility
shall be allowed to the candidates belonging to
reserved categories, such as SC/ST/OBC/Differently
abled.
(ii) Diploma / Degree Course in Teacher Education: For
the purposes of this Notification, a diploma / degree
course in teacher education recognized by the National
Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) only shall be
considered. However, in case of Diploma in
Education (Special Education) and B.Ed. (Special
Education), a course recognized by the Rehabilitation
Council of India (RCI) only shall be considered."
13. Learned Senior Counsel would also submit that CBSE is not made
a party. He would submit that the appellants cannot, in any way, succeed
having regard to the terms of the Notification and they cannot be
appointed now.
14. Mr. B.P. Nautiyal, learned Senior Counsel, would point out that the
Advertisement contemplates that a person is eligible for participating in
selection and consequentially to be appointed if he has passed TET or
CTET. He would point out that there is no challenge to the same. He
emphasised that the Advertisement, which in fact was in conformity with
the statutory rules, where also the law-giver has permitted persons having
CTET to participate in the selection process, does not stipulate and restrict
that only those persons, who have CTET prior to 2012, will be eligible to
participate. Thus, when CTET was recognised, both, under the statutory
rules and as well under the Advertisement, pursuant to which the
appellants also applied and participated in the selection process, it does
not any more lie in their mouth, now, to contend that the respondents, who
have passed CTET, may be after 2011 or 2012, are ineligible to be
considered. On this ground alone, the writ petition must be dismissed.
He also drew our attention to the reliefs sought in the writ petition and

10
contrasted it with the reliefs sought in the appeal. He would point out that
the relief, which has been sought in the writ petition, could not possibly
be granted in absence of the affected persons, namely, the current party
respondents in these appeals. The final select list having been prepared,
any direction to revise the list by eliminating the selected candidates could
not possibly have been issued without their presence on the party array.
He would also submit that the matter relating to participation in CTET is
not impermissible as both the CTET and TET stand on same footing
except the body granting the certificate, i.e. Government Government and
State Government respectively.
15. Mr. M.C. Pande, learned Additional Advocate General appearing
for the State also supported the judgment. He would, in fact, draw our
attention to the guidelines, which have been issued by NCTE, in
particular, Clause 10 thereof. He would submit that persons having CTET
certificate can also be permitted to pass muster.
16. Mr. Arvind Vashistha, learned Senior Counsel, would submit that
the respondents have obtained selection on the basis of CTET certificates.
The said certificates obtained by them are not challenged. It is on the
basis of CTET certificates that the respondents have been selected and,
what is more that they had been appointed. In the absence of any
challenge to the same, the appellants cannot succeed.
17. Mr. D.K. Joshi, learned counsel appearing for some of the
respondents, in fact, drew our attention to the guidelines issued by NCTE
for the holding of TET. The guidelines are contained in Clause 5
regarding the question relating to eligibility of the candidates. Thereafter,
we were also taken through the actual Notifications, which were issued in
terms of the said guidelines, read with Section 23(2) of the 2009 Act. We
will refer to it little later in the judgment. He would also submit that none
of the respondents were made parties in the writ petition.

11
18. Mr. D.C.S. Rawat, learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 5
in Special Appeal No. 52 of 2017 would point out that the said respondent
has obtained CTET in the year 2011 and, therefore, the said respondent,
even according to the appellants themselves, would be fully eligible.
19. Mr. V.K. Kaparwan, learned counsel appearing for respondent
No. 7 in Special Appeal No. 52 of 2017, would contend that the said
respondent has also passed CTET in the year 2011 was eligible to
participate in selection being CTET.
20. Mr. Rajesh Joshi, learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 58
in Special Appeal No. 52 of 2017, would submit that the said respondent
has passed B.Ed. and also has passed UTET in 2011 and CTET in 2011.
Therefore, the said respondent has been wrongly impleaded in the
appeals, as in either of the cases, he was eligible to participate in
selection.
21. Mr. Shiv Pandey, learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 118
in Special Appeal No. 52 of 2017, who is also respondent No. 119 in
Special Appeal No. 307 of 2016, would submit that the said respondent
has passed B.Ed. and also BTC in the year 2012, which rendered the said
respondent eligible to sit for CTET in 2015 on the basis that the said
respondent has passed BTC in 2012.
22. Mr. Yogesh Pacholia, learned counsel appearing for NCTE would
submit that the purpose of grant of CTET is to be understood from the
terms of Clause 10 of the guidelines and it is meant, essentially, for the
Central Government schools; whereas, TET imparted by State is meant
for State Government schools. He would submit that the Notifications,
which have been issued under Section 23(2) of the 2009 Act, are
essentially meant for facilitating persons obtaining TET from the State
authority.

12
23. In response to the arguments of the party respondents, Mr. Subhash
Upadhyaya in rejoinder would submit as follows:
 He would submit that, as far as reference to Clause 7.3 is
concerned, wherever there is reference to B.Ed. degree holders being
eligible, it should be understood as confined to appointment of Assistant
Teachers for Classes 6 to 8, which he submits on the basis of a perusal of
the minimum qualification, which has been laid down in Notification
dated 23.08.2010 issued by NCTE. He would submit, in other words,
that, as far as Classes 1 to 5 are concerned, with which we are concerned
in these cases, the actual qualification, apart from the minimum
qualification, which has been laid down, was Graduation with Diploma in
Elementary Education and it is, therefore, that the Note refers to, both,
Diploma and Degree and it is to be understood as meaning that it is to
apply appropriately with reference to the qualifications, which have been
fixed differently for Classes 1 to 5 on the one hand and Classes 6 to 8 on
the other hand. In other words, his submission is that in respect of
Assistant Teachers for Classes 1 to 5, B.Ed. is not a qualification laid
down and, which is available; whereas, what is available is the Diploma.
This is what, in fact, is mentioned in the Notification issued by CBSE
also. In respect of Classes 6 to 8, as per Notification dated 23.08.2010
issued by NCTE, B.Ed. is recognised as the qualification. It is only to
clarify as to what type of Diploma or B.Ed. would be considered as
eligible that reference is made to the Note and that is all and it does not
advance the case of the party respondents.
24. As far as the question posed relating to the appellants not
challenging the rules and the Advertisement, which provided for, both,
TET and CTET, Mr. Subhash Upadhyaya would submit as follows:
 He would submit that, in the rules, what is provided is that CTET
must be one, which is obtained as per NCTE standards. Having regard to
the CBSE Information Bulletin or the Advertisement, which have been
brought on record and which do not permit a B.Ed. degree holder after

13
2011 to sit for CTET, there was no need for the appellants to challenge
the law-giver's declaration that CTET is also permitted. In other words,
CTET must be one, which is as per NCTE guidelines. Insofar as CBSE,
which was the examining body and which conducted CTET, did not
include B.Ed. degree holders among the persons, who are eligible to take
the test after 2011, any person, who took CTET after 2011 could not
possibly be a person, who had CTET within the meaning of the statutory
rules or the Advertisement. In other words, again, to make it even more
clear, those persons, who had obtained CTET up to the year 2011, were
eligible. It was, in fact, pointed out by Mr. Vinay Kumar that CTET had
7 years' validity. So, the persons, who were having CTET of the year in
which it was validly obtained, could continue to utilize it for a period of 7
years from the date of issuance. So, such persons, who were having
CTET up to the year 2011, could make use of it for the selection in
accordance with the time limit within which the validity was there.
Therefore, it is submitted that there is no need to challenge the
Notifications.
25. Mr. K.P. Upadhyaya, in fact, has a case that the select list
mentioned in the writ petition had not been finalized at the time when the
writ petition was filed and it came to be finalized only much later to filing
of writ petition and hence there was no need to implead the party
respondents in these appeals as respondents in the writ petition. In fact, in
principle, an offer was made by the learned counsel for the appellants that
they may be permitted to implead CBSE also in these proceedings.
26. We have noticed the facts, and also the reliefs, which have been
sought. In fact, none of the persons, who would definitely be affected by
the grant of the relief sought for deleting the names from the select list on
the basis of the vice as alleged by the appellants, which allegedly afflicted
their selection, were made parties before the learned Single Judge. No
doubt, in the appeal, which is a continuation of the writ petition, the
appellants, who included the writ petitioners also, have taken steps on

14
being informed that a large number of persons have been appointed and
they have been made parties.
27. The clients of Mr. K.P. Upadhyaya have obtained leave and filed
the appeal. We have to take the allegations in the writ petition and the
reliefs sought by the writ petitioners as binding on them also. The
appellants in this case are not the writ petitioners. They would stand to
succeed or fail depending upon the case of the writ petitioners, as they
have no independent legs to stand on, as having failed to file an
independent writ petition at the time when cause of action accrued to them
when the selection was initiated or at least, at the time when the select list
was prepared selecting the party respondents as Assistant Teacher
(Primary). Taking the pleading as it is, we must proceed on the basis that
there was a final select list of Assistant Teachers prepared. The writ
petitioners wanted the names of those selected candidates to be removed
from the final select list, who had obtained CTET after 2011. Any such
order could definitely have been passed, if at all, only with presence of the
affected candidates. It is true, as Mr. Subhash Upadhyaya would point
out, that inclusion of persons in the select list does not confer any right
upon them; but when, as between the rival candidates, the writ petitioners
seek the removal of persons from the select list, we would think that it
may not be correct to rely on the principle that, as between the candidates
and the appointing authority, there is no indefeasible right. True it is that
they have been brought on in the party array in the appeals, for which the
appellate court is, indeed, endowed with power under law. True again it
is that appeal is a continuation of the original proceeding.
28. We may make some observations, but, having regard to the nature
of the course, which we intend to adopt, it may not be treated to be final.
29. Under section 23 of the 2009 Act, NCTE has been appointed as the
agency to declare the qualifications to be possessed by a candidate to be
appointed as a teacher at various levels. We are, in these cases, concerned
with appointment of Assistant Teachers (Primary), which means a person

15
on being appointed, who is to take classes for standards 1 to 5. In regard
to the same, the competent authority, namely, NCTE has brought out a
Notification on 23.08.2010. Various qualifications have been fixed in the
alternative and we need not be detained by them. All that is necessary for
instant case to notice is that there was a shortage of teachers possessing
the said qualifications in the State of Uttarakhand. Section 23(2) of the
2009 Act reads as follows:
 "(2) Where a State does not have adequate institutions
offering courses or training in teacher education, or teachers
possessing minimum qualifications as laid down under sub-section
(1) are not available in sufficient numbers, the Central Government
may, if it deems necessary, by notification, relax the minimum
qualifications required for appointment as a teacher, for such
period, not exceeding five years, as may be specified in that
notification: Provided that a teacher who, at the commencement of
this Act, does not possess minimum qualifications as laid down
under sub-section (1), shall acquire such minimum qualifications
within a period of five years."
30. Acting in terms thereof, State of Uttarakhand took up the matter
with the authority pointing out that there is shortage of persons, who are
having the prescribed minimum qualification; but, there are number of
persons available, who are having B.Ed. There was a positive response in
terms of power under Section 23(2) and the authority permitted persons
with B.Ed. to compete for selection as Assistant Teacher (Primary). A
period of five years is the maximum period for which the power could be
exercised under Section 23(2). Successive notifications were issued
invoking the power under Section 23(2) and the last exercise ended with
31.03.2016. Thus, with the power under Section 23(2), B.Ed. degree
holders were rendered eligible to participate in selection as Assistant
Teacher (Primary) till 31.03.2016.
31. The problem arises, however, with the undoubted requirement in
law that, be it a person who is having the minimum qualification or a
person having B.Ed., he should also possess TET conducted by the
appropriate Government in accordance with the guidelines issued by
NCTE. The respondents are all persons, except those which we have

16
made reference to earlier, who have obtained CTET. CTET is nothing but
TET, which is conducted by the Central Government. The controversy is
whether all the respondents, who have passed CTET also, therefore, under
the statutory rules, read with the Advertisement, they would, on the
surface, appear to be persons, who are fully eligible and qualified to be
appointed. But the nice controversy that is sought to be projected by the
appellants, who, it may be noted, have been worsted in the selection on
the basis of the criteria, which has been employed (which is that whether
persons with B.Ed. would be evaluated on the basis of the year of
obtaining the B.Ed.), is that, since the party respondents have obtained
CTET after 2011 and as per the conditions set out by CBSE, they were
not eligible even to participate in CTET. Therefore, their having obtained
CTET is of no avail. In fact, it is impressed upon us by the learned
counsel for the appellants that it has been mentioned in Clause 17 as
follows:
"17. It is to be noted that if a candidate has been allowed to
appear in the Central Teacher Eligibility Test it does not imply that
the candidate's eligibility has been verified. It does not vest any
right with the candidate for appointment. The eligibility shall be
finally verified, by the concerned recruiting agency/appointing
authority. The candidate should satisfy his/her eligibility before
applying and shall be personally responsible in case he/she is not
eligible to apply as per the given eligibility criteria."
32. Appellants would also remind us that the applications were given
online and there was obviously no mechanism for CBSE to weed-out
candidates, who were not eligible, and, hence, it is that the declaration
contained in Clause 17 assumes significance. It is also reflected in the
mark list. Therefore, it was the bounden duty of the State Government to
crosscheck this aspect and weed-out those, who were not really eligible to
participate in the test and it is here that the element of fraud is also
emphasized before us.
33. We may also notice, for the sake of clarity, that, after Notification
dated 23.08.2010 was issued, as in terms thereof, apparently, guidelines

17
were necessary, guidelines came to be issued on 11.02.2011. Clause 5 of
the same is extracted as under:
"5. The following persons shall be eligible for appearing in the
TET:
i. A person who has acquired the academic and
professional qualifications specified in the NCTE
Notification dated 23rd August 2010.
ii. A person who is pursuing any of the teacher education
courses (recognized by the NCTE or the RCI, as the
case may be) specified in the NCTE Notification dated
23rd August 2010.
iii. The eligibility condition for appearing in TET may be
relaxed in respect of a State/UT which has been
granted relaxation under sub-section (2) of section 23
of the RTE Act. The relaxation will be specified in the
Notification issued by the Central Government under
that sub-section."
34. It could, indeed, be said that, as far as Clause 5(i) is concerned, in
terms of Clause 3(a) of Notification dated 23.08.2010, a person with
B.Ed. was rendered eligible as he would fall within Clause 5(i) as a
person, who has acquired the academic and professional qualification
under Notification dated 23.08.2010. But, in terms of the said
Notification, it could also be said that this right came to an end on
01.01.2012. The question would arise as to what is to be the
interpretation to be placed on Clause 5(iii). Clause 5(iii) provides that the
eligibility condition for appearing in TET may be relaxed in relation to the
State / Union Territory, which has been granted relaxation under sub-section (2) of Section 23 of the 2009 Act. But the guidelines provide that
the relaxation is to be specified in the Notification issued under sub-section (2) of Section 23. There can be no doubt that, in respect of the
State of Uttarakhand, relaxation has been granted under Section 23(2) of
the 2009 Act. That is to say, in view of shortage of persons with requisite
minimum qualification and heeding to the request from the State of
Uttarakhand, persons with B.Ed. degree were rendered eligible from time
to time and, finally, culminating with the Notification for the year 2014,
by which the period was extended till 31.03.2016. In a search for the
relaxation, which is contemplated under Clause 5(iii), we did locate, in

18
Annexure-5 in the Appeal, Notification dated 17.10.2012. It does refer to
sub-clause (a) of Clause (i) of paragraph 3 of Notification dated
23.08.2010 and, obviously, refers to B.Ed. qualification and that the
Government decided to give a relaxation to the State of Uttarakhand and
allowed persons mentioned in sub-clause (a) of Clause (i) of paragraph 3.
This means that persons with B.Ed. degree, who are the persons who are
mentioned in paragraph 3, were rendered to be eligible. It was given
subject to a condition in paragraph 2, namely, that the State Government
shall conduct TET as specified in the said Notification, as amended from
time to time, in accordance with the guidelines for conducting TET. The
actual relaxation is seen granted in paragraph 3. It reads as follows:
"3. The persons referred to in sub-clause (i) of paragraph 3
of the said notification as amended from time to time, shall be
eligible for appearing in the Teacher Eligibility Test conducted by
the State Government in respect of teacher appointments made in
the State up to 31st March, 2014, in accordance with sub-paragraph
(iii) of paragraph 5 of the guidelines for conducting Teacher
Eligibility Test under the said Act issued by the Council vide its
letter dated the 11th February, 2011."
35. The appellants would, undoubtedly, point out that this paragraph
would emphasize that it is for the State Government to conduct the State
Eligibility Test and that if at all the B.Ed. degree holders were to be
rendered eligible for appearing in the TET conducted by the State
Government. This relaxation does not extend to the eligibility test, which
was being conducted by the Central Government and which awarded the
certificate called as CTET. We may also see Annexure 6, which is a
Notification issued by NCTE again under Section 23(2) dated 12.08.2014.
Therein, paragraph 3 is similarly worded as paragraph 3, which we have
extracted for the earlier years of Notification issued under Section 23(2)
of the 2009 Act. Therefore, it could undoubtedly be said that, read along
with the terms and conditions issued by CBSE, wherein B.Ed. degree
holders are conspicuous by their absence as eligible persons, the party
respondents, who had obtained CTET after 2011 were, indeed, not
eligible to sit for the test. We may in this regard also refer to paragraph

19
10 of the guidelines referred to by the learned Additional Advocate
General. It prima facie appears to us that the scheme of the guidelines is
that CTET is to be conducted by the Central Government and which will
apply to the schools referred to in sub-clause (i) of Clause (a) of Section 2
of 2009 Act. Section 2(a)(i) reads as follows:
 "2(a) "appropriate Government" means -
 (i) in relation to a school established, owned or controlled
by the Central Government, or the administrator of the Union
territory, having no legislature, the Central Government;"
36. Clause 10(b) refers to TET conducted by the State Government or a
Union Territory. It is to apply to the schools of the State
Government/Union Territory with legislature and local authority referred
to in sub-clause (i) of Clause (n) of Section 2 of the 2009 Act. Section
2(n)(i) of the 2009 Act reads as follows:
 "2(n) "school" means any recognised school imparting
elementary education and includes -
 (i) a school established, owned or controlled by the
appropriate Government or a local authority;"
37. Sub-clause (ii) of Clause 10(b) refers to a school referred to in sub-clause (ii) of Clause (n) of Section 2 of the 2009 Act. It is important to
notice that, thereafter, it is mentioned that the school at sub-clauses (i) &
(ii) may also consider the eligibility of a candidate who has obtained TET
certificate from another State / Union Territory with legislature. It is
further provided that, in case, the State Government/Union Territory with
legislature decides not to conduct TET, a school in sub-clauses (i) & (ii),
which would cover the schools with which we are concerned, namely,
State Government Schools, would consider TET conducted by the Central
Government. We had noted already that CTET is nothing but TET
conducted by the Central Government. Here, Mr. Subhash Upadhyaya
would point out that there is no scope for considering CTET granted for
the reason that it is not a case, where the State of Uttarakhand was not
conducting TET and it may be another matter that the number of tests,

20
which were conducted, were inadequate to accommodate all applicants;
but, that would not be sufficient to invoke this Clause.
38. We have referred to these arguments; but, having regard to certain
peculiar features present in this case, we feel disabled from considering
them and adjudicating on the issues, as already noticed.
39. In the Writ Petition, though the reliefs were as we have noticed, but
none of the party respondents have been impleaded. Far more
importantly, the writ petitioners were not able to obtain any interim order
at admission stage. The selections were, therefore, not faulted or slowed
down. They progressed to the stage, where, as logical and natural
culmination, persons have been favoured with appointment orders. The
party respondents before us are persons, who have admittedly been given
appointments as Assistant Teachers, though according to the appellants,
there may be persons, who have obtained CTET after the cut-off point as
alleged by the appellants. But the fact remains that their appointments
were never put in issue before the learned Single Judge and, again, what is
far more important, the appointments are not even called in question even
in the appeals, only a fact of appointment of respondents has been
pleaded. There is no application even seeking to amend the Writ Petition
(which may not be impermissible in appropriate cases) and calling in
question the appointment orders. We say this with a definite purpose, as
Mr. Subhash Upadhyaya, learned counsel, who appears for two of the writ
petitioners in the appeals, when faced with this aspect, suggested before
us that the matter may be remanded back, where necessary amendments
could be carried out. He would point out that, in the appeal, with great
difficulty, the party respondents could be finally brought on the party
array after service by publication, and, if the matter is remitted back, the
further difficulty could be avoided and the matter could be decided with
them on the party array and with amended pleadings and modified reliefs.
We did toy with this prospect also. However, noticing that the
appointments of the party respondents are even, as of today, not called in
question and they were never made parties at the original stage, but

21
noticing that there are certain crucial aspects, which are certainly required
to be adjudicated upon, we would think that, apart from making certain
modifications in the judgment of the learned Single Judge, we should
leave it free to the parties to initiate appropriate consequential proceedings
with all the affected persons on the party array and calling in question
their appointments or any such relief, if advised.
40. We cannot possibly in these circumstances spelled above, grant any
relief to the appellants in these cases, even if we accepted their case, as we
notice the cardinal fact that the appointments of the party respondents are
not called in question. Even if an appointment is illegal or even if it is
void, in proceedings of this nature, it may not be possible for us to undo
the alleged illegality in the absence of a challenge to the same, and that
too after given an opportunity to those thus appointed at the initial stage
of proceeding before the learned Single Judge, as it would have an affect
on their civil rights accrued by their appointment, and further more if
challenge to their appointment is permitted at appellate stage, there may
be a possibility that it would mar their appellate opportunity.
41. As far as the observation, which has been made by the learned
Single Judge is concerned, we may notice that there is a case for Mr. B.P.
Nautiyal, learned Senior Counsel that, having regard to the nature of the
direction given by the learned Single Judge, if at all the writ petitioners or
any appellant who had filed appeal after grant of leave, may have a fresh
cause of action, it is for them to challenge the appointment orders. We
may notice in paragraph 28 or, rather, in the judgment relating to the
appellants, the learned Single Judge has proceeded to make two
independent statements. Firstly, referring to the contention about the
ineligibility of the party respondents here, it was stated that, on the face of
it, it does not appear to be correct, as it is the Central Government body,
which has allowed B.Ed. qualified hands to take part in the selection
process till 31.03.2016. Secondly, he states that, by necessary
implication, therefore, if such candidates have passed TET, apparently,
there seems to be no anomaly unless there was any specific restriction on

22
this. The second part of the judgment is to the effect that it is exclusively
for the selection committee, who will look into this aspect before issuing
the appointment letters to such candidates. There appears to be the
statement in the judgment that it is for the selection committee, who will
look into the matter before issuing appointments orders, should there be a
specific restriction of the nature canvassed by the appellants. If this is to
be understood as the view of the learned Single Judge that the Selection
Committee will consider this aspect before appointment orders are issued
and if the specific restriction of the nature canvassed by the appellants
was, indeed, present and if this was overlooked, it certainly will furnish a
new cause of action for the appellants. As far as the statement that the
contention of the appellants / writ petitioners, on the face of it, does not
appear to be correct as it is the Central Government Body which has
permitted B.Ed. qualified hands to participate in the selection process till
31.03.2016, and the further direction that, by necessary implication,
therefore, if such candidates have passed their TET after 2011 apparently
there seems to be no anomaly, are concerned, we would think that, having
regard to the course we intend to adopt (which is to permit the appellants,
if they are so advised, to challenge the appointments, after making CBSE
also a party), the said portion of the judgment cannot be sustained. We
also feel that the statement in the judgment that, apparently, there seems
to be no anomaly may not be sustainable, as the learned Single Judge has
not really examined the merits of the appellants' case in the manner,
which we have referred to in the body of our judgment. Without
examining the actual question, namely, the effect of the guidelines, the
Notifications which were issued under Section 23(2) of the 2009 Act and
the terms and conditions which were stipulated by CBSE in the holding of
the examination for the year 2012 onwards, this finding could not have
been recorded. We, therefore, leave open the contentions of both the rival
parties. Rest of the parts of the judgment are not disturbed.
42. The appeals are, accordingly, partly allowed as above, except in
regard to respondent Nos. 5, 7, 58 and 118 in Special Appeal No. 52 of
2017. We leave it open to the appellants to call in question the

23
appointments of the party respondents in duly constituted proceedings,
wherein they may also implead CBSE apart from any other necessary and
proper party, if so advised. The judgment passed by the learned Single
Judge will stand modified as above. The appeals, however, will stand
dismissed as regards respondent Nos. 5, 7, 58 and 118 in Special Appeal
No. 52 of 2017.
